sources.title: Contrastive Learning as Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

sectionsRead: 4 Contrastive Learning as an RL Algorithm, including 4.1–4.6 and Algorithm 1 (pp. 4–7)
omissions: Text extraction does not reconstruct figure images; inspect the retained PDF for figures and equation/table layout.
Separate supplemental material availability has not been fully verified.

All seven supplied text chunks were read individually. The complete supplied 18-page conference PDF body was reviewed; its referenced Appendices A–G are absent. Appendix B proofs, C/D variant derivations, E implementation details, F/G additional results and failures, and the filtering ablation in Figure 13 were unavailable.
The extraction limitation was addressed by visually inspecting pages 1–10 and 18, all main figures and Table 1, and all six final crops. Reference pages 11–17 were read as text.

Identity/version note: the title exactly matches the catalog. The title page credits Benjamin Eysenbach; Tianjun Zhang; Sergey Levine; Ruslan Salakhutdinov. The catalog spells the final author Russ R. Salakhutdinov; the other three credits agree. The inspected artifact identifies NeurIPS 2022 but supplies no revision number/date or revision chain. This report describes this conference PDF only; no edition comparison was available.
Code, linked videos, external baseline sources and separate supplements were not inspected. No experiments were reproduced.
figuresReviewed: Figure 6 (p. 9): moving-camera curve; referenced rollout panel absent
tablesReviewed: Table 1 (p. 10): offline D4RL AntMaze, all rows and version footnote

synopsis: Contrastive RL turns discrimination between actual future states and random states into a goal-reaching critic. State-action and goal encoders produce an inner-product score; a separate actor learns actions that increase it. The exponentiated optimal score is proportional to a goal-averaged policy value. Simulated online and offline results support this approach, with restrictive proof assumptions and unavailable appendices limiting verification.

problem.text: Can an RL objective itself learn useful representations without auxiliary perception losses or image augmentation? The paper targets goal-conditioned control from action-labeled trajectories. Goals specify desired states; a probability-based reward supports the analysis, while the practical learner receives no ground-truth reward function.

contributions.text: Connects discounted future-state occupancy to goal-conditioned value, then identifies binary contrastive learning as a value estimator up to exponentiation and a goal-dependent factor.

Proposes a simple Monte Carlo-like NCE actor-critic and interprets C-learning as a TD-based contrastive method. Their combination often performs strongly, although its derivation is in absent Appendix D.
Demonstrates image-based goal reaching without auxiliary representation objectives and adapts NCE to offline data with behavioral cloning and multiple critics.

inputs: Replay trajectories with state/image observations and actions; sampled future-state positives and marginal negatives.
Current observation and commanded goal at action selection; online ant_umaze uses an XY goal.
outputs: A similarity score between a state-action pair and a candidate goal.
A goal-conditioned action distribution for environment execution.

steps.name: Construct outcome supervision
steps.detail: Sample a replay state-action pair. Its positive comes from discounted future occupancy, conceptually using a geometric time offset. A negative comes from the marginal future-state distribution of random replay pairs. Actions explicitly condition the representation of future outcomes.

steps.name: Fit a factorized critic
steps.detail: Encode the pair with phi and the goal with psi; score their inner product. Algorithm 1 forms all pairwise batch scores with positive diagonal labels and negative off-diagonal labels. It reuses goal embeddings. These are learned representations, not reconstructed future frames.

steps.name: Improve the actor and collect feedback
steps.detail: Train the neural policy on replay states and random goals to maximize critic scores through reparameterized sampled actions. Alternate critic fitting, actor updates and new experience. No learned rollout planner or inverse-dynamics decoder is specified.

training.text: Basic NCE needs no TD targets, target Q networks, multiple critics, augmentation or auxiliary representation losses. Image tasks add actor entropy. Although theoretically on-policy, the implementation reuses transitions for multiple updates as in off-policy methods.

Offline training adds lambda-weighted goal-conditioned behavioral cloning and uses the minimum of two or five critics for actor updates. Lambda equal to one recovers GCBC; the selected lambda is not supplied.

inference.text: The actor receives the current observation and desired goal and outputs actions, trained to increase their critic score. The environment supplies subsequent observations. Algorithm 1 samples actions, but the supplied body does not specify a separate deterministic-versus-stochastic evaluation convention.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): s_t and a_t are state and action, s_g is the goal, gamma the discount, and p the transition probability/density. This reward is analytical. Footnote 4 adds initial goal probability at the initial state.

Lemma 4.1: phi/psi are encoders; f* is the Bayes-optimal critic. Q belongs to the policy averaged over commanded goals; p(s_g) is the marginal negative-goal density. The raw score is a log density ratio. For a fixed goal, the denominator is independent of action.

Equation (6) maximizes this objective in expectation. Sigma is the sigmoid; s_f^+ is a sampled future state and s_f^- a marginal negative. Equation (7) trains the actor to maximize the commanded-goal score.

results.setting: Static D4RL data; NCE+BC, two versus five critics. Baseline values are quoted.
results.metric: Reported AntMaze performance; score normalization and table ± convention are unspecified.
results.comparison: GCBC 32.4; IQL 39.6; TD3+BC 0.2. Five critics exceed IQL by 9.0 table points.
results.interpretation: A substantial reported gain, but IQL/TD3+BC use v0 and no goal relabeling; this does not isolate avoiding TD.

results.setting: Same offline adaptation and table protocol.
results.metric: Reported AntMaze performance; retain source scale and unspecified ± convention.
results.comparison: GCBC 36.9; IQL 47.5. Five critics exceed IQL by 6.6 table points.
results.interpretation: The source rounds the two large-task improvements to 7–9 absolute percent.

results.setting: Same offline table; easiest listed maze.
results.interpretation: IQL wins. More critics improve four of six rows; umaze and medium-diverse decrease.

results.task: Online state- and image-based goal reaching
results.setting: Manipulation/navigation; five-seed mean and standard deviation, task-specific interaction budgets.
results.value: NCE leads most comparisons; Section 5.1 reports image sawyer_push/bin below 50%.
results.comparison: TD3+HER, GCBC and future-density modeling; the model-based method wins state ant_umaze.
results.interpretation: These are simulated control results. NCE makes progress on challenging image tasks where the listed baselines show little sustained learning.

results.setting: Four manipulation tasks, TD3+HER plus DrQ, autoencoder or CURL; five seeds.
results.value: NCE leads final performance on all four plots; endpoints are not tabulated.
results.comparison: Autoencoding helps fetch_reach and DrQ helps sawyer_push.
results.interpretation: Supports the complete algorithm here; does not exclude further benefits from augmenting NCE.

results.setting: State/image tasks; NCE, CPC, C-learning and NCE+C-learning, five seeds.
results.value: The combination often ranks among the strongest; none dominates every curve.
results.comparison: CPC changes the estimator; C-learning changes TD use and policy conditioning.
results.interpretation: A family comparison, not a controlled attribution to a single design choice.

results.setting: Camera follows the hand; the wall initially occludes the puck.
results.value: Text reports approximately 35% success; return approaches 0.35.
results.comparison: Section 5.4 quotes 75% fixed-camera success, unlike the below-50% image result in Section 5.1; protocol differences are unexplained.
results.interpretation: Learning in one partially observed setup, with unresolved metric/protocol differences and an absent referenced rollout panel.

limitations.text: Approximate policy improvement assumes tabular states/actions, a Bayes-optimal critic and trajectory filtering, with tolerance 2 gamma epsilon/(1−gamma). Main experiments omit filtering. Its reported performance penalty and the complete proof cannot be checked because Appendix Figure 13 and Appendix B are absent.
Application beyond goal-conditioned RL remains open. Occupancy similarity does not establish general world-model prediction or long-horizon planning capability.
Offline comparisons mix relabeling, ensembles and quoted protocols. The v0/v2 equivalence claim has no matched rerun here; baseline uncertainty and the table’s ± definition are missing.

reproduction.text: A faithful run needs absent Appendix E architectures, hyperparameters, preprocessing, success conventions and offline lambda. The body supplies loss code and JAX/Acme throughput on one TPUv2: 1100 batches/s for states, 105 for images, versus 28 for its DrQ. Throughput does not specify total compute or software versions.

Proposed checks should fix goal sampling, update budgets and evaluation: remove action conditioning to test the critic mechanism, then separate critic count from total capacity on an identical offline dataset version.

reasoning.text: The foundational theory/action-policy classification is supported. An occupancy-related critic and separate actor neither jointly generate futures/actions nor extract actions through inverse dynamics. The world-action-model architecture, prediction-paradigm and quadrant fields are appropriately Not applicable: an outside-quadrant foundation, not an unverified quadrant assignment.

discussionQuestions: How much practical policy improvement survives the gap between goal-averaged occupancy and the commanded-goal policy?
Would a fixed-capacity ensemble retain the offline advantage under identical dataset versions and relabeling?
Which camera protocol explains the differing static-image sawyer_push results?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title/author block, venue footer, Abstract and Section 1
evidence.detail: Exact title and credits: Benjamin Eysenbach; Tianjun Zhang; Sergey Levine; Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Affiliations: CMU; Google Research; UC Berkeley. Footer: NeurIPS 2022. Introduction frames representation learning as the RL algorithm itself.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Figure 1 and caption; p. 5, Section 4.4
evidence.detail: State-action and goal encoders feed a similarity comparison; the positive comes from the same trajectory and the illustrated negative from another. The caption says closest; Section 4.4 specifies an inner product.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Section 3, Equations (1)–(3) and footnote 4
evidence.detail: Defines goal reward as transition probability/density, discounted return/value and occupancy. Initial-state reward adds initial goal probability. The reward supports analysis rather than being estimated.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 3 continuation and Section 4.1, Proposition 1 / Equation (5)
evidence.detail: Geometric sampling gives discounted occupancy. Combining commanded goals defines an averaged policy. Goal-conditioned Q equals corresponding discounted goal occupancy.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 4.2, Equation (6), Lemma 4.1 and following paragraphs
evidence.detail: Replay state-action pairs are contrasted with conditional future states and marginal negatives. The optimal log density-ratio score exponentiates to goal-averaged-policy Q divided by marginal goal density.
The neural actor takes state and goal, samples actions and maximizes critic scores through reparameterization gradients. Image tasks add entropy. Training alternates critic, actor and collection.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Algorithm 1, Section 4.4 continuation and final summary paragraph
evidence.detail: Batch dot products use identity-matrix binary labels; actor maximizes paired logits. NCE is theoretically on-policy but reuses transitions. It needs no target network, multiple Q values or auxiliary image machinery. JAX/Acme and single-TPUv2 throughput are stated; architecture/hyperparameters are deferred to Appendix E.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4.5, trajectory exclusion rule and Lemma 4.2
evidence.detail: Assumes tabular states/actions, Bayes-optimal critic and epsilon filtering of trajectory likelihood ratios; approximate improvement allows loss 2 gamma epsilon/(1−gamma). Main experiments omit filtering. Appendix B and Figure 13 are referenced but absent.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Sections 4.6 and 5.1, Figure 3 and footnote 8
evidence.detail: C-learning uses TD and commanded-goal policy occupancy, unlike NCE averaging. Baselines: TD3+HER, GCBC, normalized future-density modeling. Figure 3 shows simulated task environments.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 2; p. 8, Section 5.1 Tasks and results paragraphs
evidence.detail: State/image manipulation, image point navigation and 111-dimensional ant locomotion with XY goals are evaluated. Five-seed means/standard deviations are plotted. NCE leads most tasks, model-based wins state ant_umaze, and image Sawyer push/bin are described as below 50%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figure 4 and Section 5.2; p. 9, Section 5.2 continuation
evidence.detail: Four image-task curves compare NCE with TD3+HER plus DrQ, AE or CURL. NCE leads final performance without augmentation/auxiliary objectives; authors do not rule out further representation-learning benefits.

NCE, CPC, C-learning and their combination are compared with five-seed mean/standard deviation curves. The combination often ranks strongly, with task-dependent exceptions. Appendices C/D derivations are absent.

Camera follows the hand; the puck is initially occluded. Text reports about 35% success and 75% with fixed camera. The graph is labeled return. The referenced left rollout panel is absent from the supplied figure.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 5.5, offline actor objective and Table 1 footnote
evidence.detail: Offline NCE adds lambda-weighted goal-conditioned BC and uses the minimum of two or five critics. Quoted TD3+BC/IQL results use v0 while table tasks use v2; footnote claims negligible TD impact. Normalization, lambda value and table ± definition are not specified.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 1, large-play-v2 and large-diverse-v2 rows, GCBC / Contrastive RL+BC / IQL columns
evidence.detail: Large-play: GCBC 32.4, two critics 41.6 ±6.0, five 48.6 ±4.4, IQL 39.6, TD3+BC 0.2. Large-diverse: GCBC 36.9, two 49.3 ±6.3, five 54.1 ±5.5, IQL 47.5. Five-critic minus IQL differences are 9.0 and 6.6 table points.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 1, all rows; particularly umaze-v2 and medium-diverse-v2
evidence.detail: Umaze: two critics 81.9 ±1.7, five 79.8 ±1.4, IQL 87.5, GCBC 65.4. Medium-diverse decreases from 72.5 ±2.8 to 71.5 ±1.3. Five critics improve four rows. A contrastive configuration exceeds all baselines on five rows. Baseline uncertainty is absent.
Application to arbitrary RL objectives and stronger contrastive algorithms remain open; authors limit this work to goal-conditioned RL.
Proofs are deferred to Appendix B and training details to E. Code is promised upon acceptance. Figure error bars are five-seed mean/standard deviation. Compute answer points to TPUv2 throughput.
